profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between a university urban ecology lead and a municipal landscape strategist to organize the first six-week pilot phase of a Swedish transdisciplinary lawn research project in Malmö. The pilot will combine ecological fieldwork, municipal planning data, and a stakeholder workshop to develop a shared conceptual framework for how different kinds of lawns function socially and ecologically across public urban space. The agenda is to decide how many pilot sites to include, what existing municipal material will be assembled, who should be invited to the first stakeholder workshop, and what must be finished before the June workshop date. The expected outcome is an agreed pilot plan covering site selection, data assembly, workshop preparation, and rough responsibilities without getting into detailed research design.

members.name: Dr. Elin Söderberg
members.expertise: Urban vegetation ecology, field sampling design, biodiversity indicators in managed green spaces
members.background: Elin is a senior researcher at a Swedish university coordinating the ecological side of the lawn project and has previously run comparative studies of mowing regimes in parks and housing landscapes.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to produce ecologically defensible comparative material quickly, and is worried that the project's transdisciplinary ambition could turn the first phase into a broad dialogue exercise before solid ecological baselines are in place.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says a 'site,' it means one contiguous lawn unit with a single mowing and management regime, because that is the only ecologically comparable sampling unit.
The first stakeholder round should mainly involve actors who directly shape maintenance decisions, such as parks managers and contractors, not general users of the spaces.
A 'baseline' is not truly ready until each selected lawn unit has had at least one field visit with vegetation notes and basic soil compaction measurements.
The phrase 'mowing data' naturally refers to dated records of what cuts were actually carried out, not just planned maintenance classes.
If the workshop is in June, the baseline material feeding it should already include the first ecological observations rather than being mostly desk-based.

members.name: Karin Holm
members.role: Municipal Landscape Strategist and Stakeholder Liaison
members.expertise: Urban green-space planning, municipal maintenance systems, participatory planning across public-space departments
members.background: Karin works in Malmö's streets and parks administration and often translates between municipal operations, consultants, and research partners on externally funded sustainability projects.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to fit municipal timelines and produce something colleagues can immediately use, and is concerned that too much emphasis on field ecology early on will delay practical engagement with planners and local actors.
hidden_assumptions: When people discuss a 'site,' they usually mean a recognizable place such as a park, schoolyard, or cemetery area, even if that place contains several separate lawn patches.
A 'stakeholder workshop' in a transdisciplinary project naturally includes not only municipal staff but also residents, institutional landholders, and other everyday users tied to the spaces.
A project 'baseline' is ready once existing maps, maintenance categories, photos, and planning context are assembled well enough to support discussion; ecological sampling can deepen it afterward.
The standard municipal object called 'mowing data' is the maintenance-class layer and tender documentation that specifies intended cutting frequencies for each area.
A June workshop can be used to sharpen the research framing itself, so all field-based material does not need to be complete beforehand.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as one pilot site
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to work with '12 sites' in the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 understands this as 12 ecologically homogeneous lawn units, each with one management regime and one sampling protocol.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 understands this as 12 named places in the city, such as parks or school grounds, each of which may contain multiple different lawn areas.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Using a round number of 'sites' feels routine and cooperative in planning talk, and both assume their own professional unit of analysis is the obvious one behind the word.

misalignment_points.topic: Who belongs in the first stakeholder workshop
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to run a 'first stakeholder workshop' for the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the workshop is limited to maintenance decision-makers and municipal or contractor actors who can explain management logic and access to operational data.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the workshop also includes residents, school representatives, cemetery staff, housing-company managers, and other non-municipal actors connected to lawn use and expectations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both strongly endorse stakeholder involvement, so the phrase sounds aligned; the boundary of who is included in the first round feels like background context rather than something needing explicit negotiation.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'last year's mowing data' refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Karin will pull 'last year's mowing data' for the selected areas.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects dated records of actual mowing events from 2024 contractor logs or machine reports that show what was really done on the ground.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 intends to provide the municipality's latest maintenance-class GIS layer and procurement specifications, which colleagues casually call mowing data because they govern mowing frequency.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In municipal-research collaboration, both artifacts are routinely described with the same shorthand, and neither speaker has reason to suspect the other means a different document set.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for the baseline to be ready by June
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the 'baseline should be ready by the June workshop.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks readiness means each pilot lawn unit has already had its first ecological field pass and enough measurements to anchor comparisons before workshop materials are finalized.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks readiness means a coherent planning-and-management overview is assembled so participants can react to it in June, even if ecological fieldwork is still underway afterward.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the same project-management phrase and assume their own discipline's standard sequencing is normal, so surface agreement on timing masks different thresholds for completion.

turns.inner_thought: If we can settle the structure now, I can keep this from drifting into a broad co-creation exercise before we have anything ecologically solid. Twelve sites is manageable if each site is one discrete lawn unit with a single mowing regime. And if the baseline should be ready by the June workshop, that has to mean we've already been out once to every selected unit for vegetation notes and basic compaction, otherwise we're discussing abstractions.
turns.utterance: I think the main thing today is to lock the Malmö pilot structure so we can move efficiently toward the June workshop. If we can agree on 12 sites and what counts as a usable baseline, the rest of the planning should become much easier.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, we need something concrete that municipal colleagues immediately recognize. Twelve sites makes sense if they are identifiable places across different city contexts—parks, school grounds, roadside greens, cemetery areas—because then people can picture them and see why they matter. If we make it too narrow too early, it will be hard to get internal buy-in.
turns.utterance: I agree. From the municipal side, it would be good if the 12 sites give us a spread of recognizable contexts in the city—parks, school grounds, roadside greens, cemetery areas—so the pilot feels representative and legible to colleagues straight away.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as long as within those contexts the 12 sites are still ecologically comparable units. I need them grouped by mowing regime and social setting so field observations can start cleanly and quickly. If each site is internally mixed, the comparison will be messy from day one.
turns.utterance: That sounds workable. From my side, it would help if we can think about the 12 sites in a way that gives us a spread across mowing regime and social setting as well, so each site can support comparable observations from the outset.

turns.inner_thought: Once we have the list of places, I can easily assemble the standard material from our systems. Last year's mowing data, in the way we use the term internally, will be the maintenance-class layer plus the procurement and tender information on intended cutting frequency. That should be enough to get the overview going.
turns.utterance: Good. Once we settle the list, I can pull last year's mowing data and the location material from the city system, so we have a package to work from fairly quickly.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—if I can get actual records of what cuts were carried out last year, we can check that each lawn unit really fits the intended category before the first field pass. That will help make the baseline genuinely defensible before June.
turns.utterance: That would be very helpful. If we have last year's mowing data early, we can match each site to what was actually done before the first ecological pass, which will make the baseline much stronger.

turns.inner_thought: We also need the first workshop to reflect the transdisciplinary setup, not just internal operations. Parks staff, yes, but also a few housing-company managers, school representatives, maybe someone from the cemetery side, and ideally people connected to everyday use of these places. That will help shape the framing while it's still open.
turns.utterance: On the workshop, I think the first stakeholder workshop should include parks staff, but also a few housing-company managers, school representatives, and perhaps a cemetery contact, so the conversation covers how the sites are expected to function in practice.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the people in the room are those closest to maintenance decisions, that should be useful. I don't want the first round diluted by general user perspectives before we even know the management histories properly. The pilot still needs to be structured around operational logic.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. It will be useful in the first stakeholder workshop to hear from the people closest to the maintenance decisions while the pilot is still taking shape.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then we're aligned. For me the baseline should be ready by June if we have something coherent enough for discussion—maps, maintenance categories, photos, planning context—for each place. Ecological sampling can continue afterward and deepen the picture once people have reacted.
turns.utterance: Exactly. And if the baseline should be ready by the June workshop, then participants can react to maps, maintenance categories, and photos for each site during the session, which would give us a useful starting point.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, June is fine, but only if I can get a first field visit completed at all 12 lawn units before anything is finalized for the workshop. Otherwise the baseline will be mostly desk-based, and that is exactly what I want to avoid in this first phase.
turns.utterance: I agree on the June timing. I’ll plan the first round of visits so the baseline for the 12 sites is in place before the workshop materials are finalized.

turns.inner_thought: Great. I'll draft the list of 12 places and the invitees this week, and I can attach the mowing data package from our system so Elin's team can start making site sheets. That should keep things moving on municipal timelines and give us something concrete to circulate.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Then I’ll draft the place list and the invitees this week, and I’ll attach the mowing data package as well so your team can start organizing site sheets.
